lesson.title: The Rise of the Common Man: Jacksonian Democracy Remakes Politics
lesson.summary: Fueled by expanded voting rights and outrage over the disputed election of 1824, Jacksonian Democracy reshaped American politics around mass parties and populist appeals to the ordinary white male voter.
lesson.body:
Jacksonian Democracy refers to the political movement and style associated with Andrew Jackson's rise to the presidency, roughly spanning the 1820s through the 1840s. It celebrated the ordinary white male citizen as the proper source of political power, distrusted concentrated wealth and inherited privilege, and pushed for the expansion of democratic participation well beyond what the founding generation had imagined.

Much of this shift happened at the state level in the years after the War of 1812, as one state after another dropped property requirements for voting and officeholding, expanding the electorate to nearly all adult white men. This expansion had nothing to do with race or gender, since it did not extend to women, enslaved people, or, in most states, free Black men, some of whom actually lost voting rights they had previously held as states rewrote their constitutions. Political parties adapted to the larger electorate by building mass organizations, holding public rallies, and campaigning directly for popular votes rather than relying on elite maneuvering within legislatures.

The turning point came in the election of 1824. Andrew Jackson won the most popular votes and the most electoral votes among four Democratic-Republican candidates, but not a majority, throwing the election into the House of Representatives under the Twelfth Amendment. Speaker of the House Henry Clay, who had finished fourth and was eliminated from consideration, threw his support behind John Quincy Adams, who won the House vote. When Adams then named Clay his secretary of state, traditionally a stepping stone to the presidency, Jackson and his supporters denounced the arrangement as a corrupt bargain, and Jackson spent the next four years building a political movement aimed at winning the presidency outright.

That movement became the Democratic Party, and it triumphed in the election of 1828, when Jackson defeated Adams in a landslide built on the newly expanded electorate and a far more aggressive style of campaigning, including local committees, partisan newspapers, and public rallies that treated Jackson as a champion of the common man against a distant, elitist government. Supporters of Adams and Clay eventually organized themselves into the Whig Party during the 1830s, giving the country a genuine two party system again after the one party calm of the Era of Good Feelings.

Jacksonian Democracy left a complicated legacy. It genuinely broadened political participation and made American politics more openly competitive and popular in style than it had been under the founding generation. At the same time, its vision of democracy for the common man excluded women, Native Americans, and Black Americans, whether enslaved or free, and Jackson's own presidency would show how the same appeal to popular will could justify forcibly removing Native nations from their land and concentrating executive power in ways earlier generations had feared.
